body_markdown:
By 1966, Lotus Formula 1 cars had long established that putting the engine behind the driver was the fastest way to get around a racetrack. In the hands of Sir Stirling Moss, the Lotus 18 won the 1960 Monaco Grand Prix and there was no turning back.


However, it would not be until the launch of the[Europa](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/the-ups-and-downs-of-the-europas-nose/) that the Lotus road cars would take on the same layout. It was Britain’s first mid-engined sports car, setting a precedent for almost every Lotus (Elite and EVs aside) that has followed.


A steel backbone provided the chassis, while the fiberglass breadvan bodywork was definitely designed with function over form in mind. In early cars the body was bonded to the chassis for extra rigidity, but in the interest of cost savings, that led to the system being replaced by simple bolts. For suspension, the Europa used wishbones with coilover dampers up front, and the Elan’s Chapman strut rear end, which originated in single-seaters.


It may have had had a race-derived platform, but when it came out, the Europa didn’t exactly pack an F1 punch. Power came from a 1.5-liter four-pot, mated to a four-speed transaxle transmission, both sourced from the Renault 16. Just 77 horsepower was on tap, but in the typical style of Lotus founder Colin Chapman, the Europa offset this by being ridiculously lightweight. The Type 46 Series 1 tipped the scales at a svelte 612 kg, or 1349 pounds. That’s about a thousand pounds less than a base 2026 Mazda Miata.


Lotus


The Series 2 (Type 54) squeezed another five horses out of the Renault engine, but it wasn’t until the arrival of the Twin-Cam Type 74 that the Europa topped 100 horses, thanks to its Ford-sourced and Lotus-polished 1.6-liter motor.


Primarily a road car, the Europa nonetheless served Lotus well on the track. The Type 47 won during its first outing at Brands Hatch in 1966, and was victorious in eight races in 1967. It also formed the basis of the Type 62 race car, designed to compete against other sports prototypes. Just two were built and raced a total of 30 times between them, with a best finish of third.


It’s this duo that inspired what is, without doubt, the most extreme Europa ever made: The Banks model, modified by Banks Engineering.


With its wide body, fat rear tires, side skirts, splitters, and jumbo-jet rear wing, it certainly stands out amongst the dozen-or-so other Europas lined up at the Concours of Elegance at Hampton Court Palace, located 12 miles from central London, marking the Europa’s 60th anniversary.


Owner Mark Edwards takes up the story: “I think 26 race cars by Banks were built in the mid-1990s that went out to Japan for racing, and then they built, I think, about four or five road-going versions of that race car,” which was a homage to the Type 62 1969 Lotus racer.


Like those race cars, the Banks Europa uses a spaceframe chassis with wishbone suspension all around featuring adjustable coilovers, and the brakes are upgraded to vented discs at each corner. In fact, very little of the donor Europa remains. “I think only the chassis badge and windscreen are original, but it’s still registered as a 1969 Europa,” says Edwards.


[Nik Berg](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nberg/)


“I think there’s one in Japan, the Netherlands, the U.S., this one, and possibly one in Australia. It’s powered by a two-liter, 16-valve Vauxhall Redtop engine with about 185 brake horsepower. The reason it’s got the Vauxhall engine in it is because the Type 62 original 1969 race cars had an experimental Vauxhall four-pot engine, so this is a bit of a nod to that.”


It weighs in at just 1832 pounds and is “very fast and sounds like a race car,” enthuses Edwards.


[Nik Berg](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nberg/)


“It was built by a private owner, in conjunction with Banks, but he died, I think, 400 miles after it was built,” he continues. “His wife sold it at Bonhams in 2022, and then the next owner bought it and upgraded the throttle bodies. He spent about £5000 on it,” which is about $6700 at today’s exchange rate, “and put 700 miles on it. Then it sat in the back of his garage. I found it with 1100 miles on it, and I bought it last November.


“I’ve always liked the Europa, and I was looking for one because I had a Marcos GT, which I’ve shown here three times, but I’ve fallen out a bit with the Marcos crowd. I’ve always liked Lotus, and the Lotus gang is lovely. So, then I spotted this on PistonHeads,” a British enthusiast website, and he went up to Cheshire to look at it. “The guy started it, we both laughed, I shook his hand, and he delivered it to me a couple of weeks later, and I’ve been having fun in it ever since.”
